name: Scandinavian, Icelandic Gambit
summary: The Icelandic Gambit is a sharp Scandinavian where Black plays 3...e6 to sacrifice a pawn for rapid development and open lines.
intro: The Icelandic Gambit arises after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6, when instead of regaining the pawn Black offers a second one with 4.dxe6 Bxe6, gaining a big lead in development and open lines against White's centre and the f2-point.
line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 c4 e6 dxe6 Bxe6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: Rather than the routine recapture on d5, Black treats the position as a genuine gambit, using the time White spends grabbing and holding the pawn to develop rapidly with ...Bc5, ...Nc6, ...O-O and ...Qe7 or ...Qd7. The open e-file and active bishops give real, lasting compensation.

Black's pieces swarm toward d4, f2 and White's uncastled king, so White must develop with great care and avoid greedy pawn-grabbing. If White consolidates and returns the pawn at the right moment the extra material can tell, but one careless move can leave the king caught in the centre.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 4.dxe6 Bxe6 Black develops with tempo, hitting the c4-pawn with the bishop and following up with ...Nc6, ...Bc5 and quick castling. White commonly returns the pawn to blunt the initiative and reach a roughly balanced game, or tries to hold on and weather the attack.

Key target squares for Black are d4 and f2, and moves like ...Bb4+ or ...Qe7 add to the pressure. White's soundest approach is patient development, timely returns of material and getting the king to safety before Black's activity becomes decisive.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The gambit is associated with Icelandic players who developed and popularised it, and it is also known as the Icelandic-Palme Gambit. It belongs to the dynamic wing of Scandinavian theory, prized by attacking players who happily invest a pawn for the initiative and are willing to play for the attack straight out of the opening.
